Stretchtext: the 1967 idea that waited for generated text

Fixture page for StretchText tests. Not a real article.

In 1967 Ted Nelson described stretchtext, text that grows where the reader wants more and shrinks back where they don't. The idea was simple and the demo was convincing, but it never caught on in practice. Every level of detail had to exist before the reader arrived, so authors quietly went back to writing one fixed version of everything.

The economics flipped once text could be generated on demand. Now the short version is the only one anyone has to write in advance, and the expansions are produced at the moment a reader asks, in place, exactly where the question came up. This fixture paragraph is long enough to qualify for the stretch control, unlike the short ones around it.

Short paragraph. It should not get a control.

Code blocks are never touched. p.stretch { content: "no"; }

Editable text is never touched either, even when it is long enough to look like an article paragraph with several sentences in it. StretchText skips anything the reader can type into, by design, every time.
